script.opening: "Morning, doctor. So my swallowing’s been a bit off — food seems to stick when it goes down, especially bread and a bit of steak. I’ve started cutting things up small and taking my time. It’s probably just my reflux acting up, or getting old, isn’t it? I just wondered if you could give me something stronger than the antacids from the chemist. I’ve lost a bit of weight too but I could do with losing it anyway, ha."

facts.text: If explored: PROGRESSIVE difficulty swallowing solids over ~6 weeks — started with bread/meat, food physically "sticks", now adapting how he eats (cutting small, eating slowly). Progressive dysphagia to solids is a red flag for oesophageal pathology/cancer until proven otherwise.

On questioning: ~7 kg unintentional weight loss (he jokes it off), long reflux history, 30 pack-year smoking, ~30 units alcohol/week — all risk factors for oesophageal cancer. Possibly more tired; if asked, occasional discomfort behind the sternum on swallowing.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the jokey minimising masks real fear and a specific dread: a friend recently died of "throat cancer" that "started with food sticking", and Brian is privately terrified it’s the same, so he’s reframing it as harmless ageing/reflux and asking for tablets to avoid the truth. The humour ("could do with losing it") is a shield.
If reached: ex-publican, drinking and smoking history he feels guilty about; widower who now eats alone and has "let himself go"; frightened both of cancer and of being told his lifestyle caused it.

Officially: stronger antacids. What he needs: recognition that progressive dysphagia with weight loss needs an upper-GI suspected cancer pathway referral (regardless of age), delivered so he accepts it despite his fear, without a shaming lifestyle lecture.

ice.ideas: It’s just his reflux or getting older; stronger antacids will sort it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a friend recently died of "throat cancer" that started with food sticking; he’s terrified it’s the same and is reframing it as harmless to avoid the truth, with guilt about his smoking/drinking.
ice.expectations: Stronger indigestion tablets. What he actually needs: an upper-GI suspected cancer pathway referral, usually straight to endoscopy (OGD), with his fear addressed and no shaming.

cues: "Food sticks, I’ve started cutting it up small" — progressive dysphagia to solids; a red flag, not reflux.
"Lost weight but could do with it, ha" — unintentional weight loss joked away; the shield over real fear.
Reflux + smoking + alcohol history — oesophageal-cancer risk factors stacking up.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PROGRESSIVE DYSPHAGIA TO SOLIDS as a red flag for oesophageal/upper-GI cancer until proven otherwise, and does NOT accept the "reflux/getting older" reframe or simply escalate antacids

States the NICE NG12 pathway clearly: dysphagia at ANY age warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7, amended 2025, which replaced urgent direct-access OGD within 2 weeks); he also meets the second limb (aged 55 and over with weight loss and reflux); restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12 — and does not require him to "fail" a PPI trial first given dysphagia (the NICE CG184 reflux pathway of PPI trial and H. pylori testing does not apply once dysphagia is present)

Weights the supporting features and risk factors: unintentional weight loss (at 55 and over, with upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia, a suspected cancer pathway referral criterion in itself under NICE NG12, updated April 2026), long-standing reflux (Barrett’s risk), smoking and alcohol — building the case for urgency

Takes a focused history to characterise the dysphagia (solids vs liquids, progressive vs intermittent, level, odynophagia, regurgitation) and checks for anaemia (FBC, with U&E if intake is poor and LFTs), weight/BMI, neck and supraclavicular nodes and an epigastric/abdominal mass in person, without delaying the suspected cancer pathway referral
Knows what would escalate to emergency (complete obstruction/inability to swallow saliva, food bolus, significant bleeding/haematemesis, severe dehydration) and safety-nets for it
Hears the humour as a shield and surfaces the friend’s death gently; does not collude with "just reflux" nor frighten him off; balances honesty with the fact a cause will be found and acted on

Addresses smoking/alcohol (UK CMOs 2016: at or below 14 units a week; record his ~30 units accurately) and any guilt WITHOUT a shaming lecture — supportive, blame-light, and focused on getting him assessed

Safety-nets and follows up: explains the suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12; usually straight to OGD; NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral) and what to expect, what to do if he cannot swallow at all / vomits blood, ensures he attends, documents, and arranges to follow up the result

worked.txt: "I’m glad you mentioned the swallowing, because I can’t just give you stronger antacids for that — and I’ll tell you why honestly. Food physically sticking, getting steadily worse so you’re cutting it small, plus weight coming off — that’s not simple reflux or just age. That combination we always check urgently."

"The right thing here is a camera test of your gullet and stomach — an endoscopy — and because of the swallowing and weight loss, you qualify for the urgent suspected cancer pathway — usually straight to a quick camera test. That’s what the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, says for swallowing trouble at any age. It’s how we find the cause and sort it, not me saying the worst."

"Can I gently ask — has anything in particular been worrying you about this? … Your friend, with the throat cancer that started the same way. I’m so sorry. That makes total sense of why ‘reflux and tablets’ felt easier to say. But it’s exactly why we look now — so you know, rather than dread."

"You mentioned the pub years, the smoking and a drink — I’m not here to give you a hard time about any of that. It’s relevant, yes, but my job today is getting you seen, not lecturing you. We can talk about cutting down later, gently, when you’re ready."

"Most causes of this can be treated — sometimes it’s a narrowing from years of acid, sometimes inflammation — and yes, sometimes something we’d want to catch early, which is the point of going fast. I’ll also do a blood count today. Let’s get the camera test arranged."

"If you reach the point where you can’t swallow even your spit, food gets completely stuck, or you vomit blood — that’s A&E straight away, don’t wait for the appointment. Keep to softer foods and small amounts meanwhile. I’ll chase the endoscopy and we’ll go through whatever it shows together. You came for tablets; what you’re getting is a proper answer, quickly."

f.learning: Progressive dysphagia to solids is a red flag for oesophageal/upper-GI malignancy until proven otherwise — and the NICE NG12 rule is unambiguous: dysphagia at ANY age warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (this replaced urgent direct-access endoscopy in the 2025 amendment), with no requirement to trial a PPI first (the NICE CG184 reflux pathway does not apply once dysphagia is present); he also meets the second limb (55 or over with weight loss and reflux). Do not accept a "reflux/getting older" reframe or simply escalate antacids. Supporting features sharpen the urgency: unintentional weight loss, long-standing reflux (Barrett’s risk), smoking and alcohol. Characterise the dysphagia (solids vs liquids, progressive vs intermittent, odynophagia, regurgitation), check an FBC, and know the emergency escalations (complete obstruction, food bolus, haematemesis). The examinable hidden agenda is fear masked by humour — a friend who died of "throat cancer" that "started with food sticking" — plus guilt about a smoking/drinking history. Surface the fear gently, address lifestyle without shaming, balance honesty with the fact a cause will be found and treated, and complete the suspected cancer pathway referral with a clear safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
knowledge.summary: Six weeks of progressive difficulty swallowing solids with 7 kg unintended weight loss is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise. NICE NG12 calls for a suspected cancer pathway referral for dysphagia at any age — no PPI trial first, and not stronger antacids.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7 (amended 2025): refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. This replaced the earlier urgent direct-access endoscopy route. Brian meets both limbs.

Food sticking that has worsened from solids over weeks points to a mechanical narrowing — tumour or peptic stricture. Intermittent difficulty with both solids and liquids from the start suggests a motility problem. Ask about level, pain on swallowing, regurgitation, cough on swallowing and liquids.

Long-standing reflux (Barrett’s oesophagus and adenocarcinoma), 30 pack-years of smoking and heavy drinking (squamous cell carcinoma), male sex and age. Their presence adds urgency; their absence would not remove it.

points.h: Do not treat it as reflux
points.t: NICE CG184 manages uncomplicated dyspepsia and reflux with lifestyle advice, a PPI trial and H. pylori testing. That pathway does not apply once dysphagia is present — escalating acid suppression delays the diagnosis.
In person: weight and BMI, hydration, neck and supraclavicular nodes, epigastric mass. FBC for anaemia, U&E if intake is poor, LFTs. None of this should hold up the endoscopy request.
Unable to swallow saliva, food stuck and not passing, vomiting blood or significant dehydration — same-day emergency assessment, not the suspected cancer pathway.
UK CMOs (2016): regular drinking should stay at or below 14 units a week. Record intake accurately and offer support later; a lecture now risks losing a frightened man from the pathway.

dg.d: Open question on the swallowing; did not jump to prescribing; noted the joked-about weight loss for later.
Retired publican, smoking and alcohol history asked without blame, eating alone as a widower, how meals are going.
Face-to-face weight, abdominal and neck examination; FBC, U&E, LFTs; suspected cancer pathway referral (often straight to OGD).
Oesophageal or gastric cancer, peptic stricture, oesophagitis, motility disorder; progressive solid-food dysphagia weighed as mechanical.
Checked liquids and saliva, level, odynophagia, regurgitation, weight, bleeding; knows complete obstruction or haematemesis means same-day care.
States a suspected upper GI cancer picture needing an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral, not reflux, in plain language and without false certainty.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer; no PPI trial first; referral sent today.
Soft diet, weight monitoring and dietitian if needed; alcohol recorded and support offered later without shaming.
A&E triggers named, ring if no hospital date within a week, GP reviews the result, teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: The laugh about weight, “it’s my own fault”, and the friend who died — each explored rather than passed over.
Idea (reflux or ageing), the hidden concern (the same throat cancer as his friend, and guilt), expectation of stronger antacids.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a friend recently died of "throat cancer" that started with food sticking; he’s terrified it’s the same and is reframing it as harmless to avoid the truth, with guilt about his smoking/drinking — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Mr Halloran, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me all right, and are you somewhere you can talk? … Lovely. Tell me about the swallowing.
model.why: Checks the video set-up then opens on his main symptom

model.text: Food sticks going down — bread, a bit of steak. I’ve started cutting it small. It’s my reflux, or getting old. I just want something stronger than the chemist’s stuff. Lost a bit of weight too, but I could do with losing it, ha.

I’ll come to the tablets, I promise. Can I spend a few minutes understanding the swallowing properly first, then we’ll decide together what’s best? And I noticed the weight — I’d like to come back to that too.
model.why: Agrees an agenda and flags the weight loss he joked away

model.text: Go on, then.
When did you first notice food sticking, and has it stayed the same or got worse?
About six weeks. It’s definitely worse. Started with bread, now meat too. Soup’s fine.
Where do you feel it stick — point to it for me? And is it painful when it goes down, or does food ever come back up?
Round here, behind the breastbone. A bit uncomfortable sometimes. It doesn’t come back up.
Can you still swallow drinks and your own saliva without trouble?
model.why: Screens for complete obstruction — an emergency

model.text: Yes, drinks are fine.
And the weight — roughly how much, over what time? Any vomiting blood, or black stools?
model.why: Quantifies weight loss and screens for bleeding

model.text: Seven kilos, maybe — my trousers are loose. No blood. Bit more tired.
Thank you. Tell me a bit about day-to-day life — do you smoke or drink these days?
Gave up the fags years ago — thirty years of them, mind. I ran a pub. I still like a drink. About thirty units a week, I reckon. I know, I know.
You don’t need to apologise to me. I noticed you laughed about the weight — can I ask, has anything in particular been worrying you about all this?
model.why: Removes blame and reads the humour as a cue

model.text: …A mate of mine. Throat cancer. Died not long ago. His started with food sticking. I keep telling myself mine’s just reflux.
I’m so sorry about your friend. That makes complete sense of why reflux felt like the safer word. It must have been sitting heavily on you.
model.why: Validates the fear behind the minimising

model.text: It has. And I suppose if it is something, it’s my own fault, isn’t it? The pub, the smoking.
I’m not here to blame you for anything. What matters today is getting you seen quickly.

So I’ll be honest with you. Food sticking that’s getting steadily worse, plus seven kilos gone without trying, isn’t ordinary reflux or age. Stronger antacids would just cover it up. What you need is a camera test of your gullet and stomach — an endoscopy.
model.why: Declines the reflux reframe and names the investigation

model.text: So it is what I thought.

It might not be. Narrowing from years of acid is common and treatable, and so is inflammation. But national guidance is clear: anyone with swallowing trouble gets an urgent referral on the suspected cancer pathway, which usually means a quick camera test — that’s about being sure quickly, not a verdict.
model.why: States the NICE NG12 dysphagia criterion (a suspected cancer pathway referral) and what happens next, balanced honestly

model.text: I’d also like to see you in person — to weigh you, feel your tummy and neck — and take a blood count and some routine bloods. None of that will hold up the referral; I’ll send it today.
model.why: Examination and bloods alongside, not instead of, the referral

model.text: How are you managing with meals at the moment, day to day?
model.why: Explores the practical and nutritional impact

model.text: Since the wife passed I mostly eat on my own. Easier to skip it, if I’m honest.

That’s useful to know. Until the test, go for softer, moist food — soups, stews, mash, yoghurt — little and often, and take your time. If the weight keeps dropping we can get dietitian advice. And the drink — we can talk about cutting down another day, when you’re ready. Today is about the test.
model.why: Practical interim plan; defers the alcohol conversation without ignoring it

model.text: That’s fair. I’d rather know than keep guessing.

If food gets stuck and won’t go down, you can’t swallow your own spit, or you vomit blood — go to A&E straight away, don’t wait for the appointment. The hospital will phone you with a date; if you haven’t heard within a week, ring me.
model.why: Emergency triggers and a clear fallback if the appointment doesn’t come

model.text: Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
Camera test in the next two weeks, bloods and a check-up with you, soft food meantime, and A&E if it all gets stuck or I bring up blood.
Perfect. I’ll go through the result with you myself. Thank you for telling me about your friend — it helps.
model.why: Commits to follow-up and closes with warmth

social.t: A widower who now eats alone and skips meals is at risk of further weight loss and dehydration while he waits; give simple soft-diet advice and watch his weight.

A lifetime in the pub trade shapes how he sees his drinking. Record units accurately, avoid blame, and offer brief intervention or support when he is ready (UK CMOs 2016: no more than 14 units a week).

legal.t: If sedation is used for the endoscopy he must not drive home; the unit will say how long to avoid driving. There is no DVLA notification for the investigation itself.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): see the patient in person when remote assessment cannot meet their needs safely — weight and examination here — without letting it delay the referral.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share what he needs to know honestly and at his pace, without false reassurance. Document the red flags, the referral and the safety-net.
Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals to confirm he is seen; the doctor who refers owns the follow-up of the result.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support and Guts UK for information while waiting; local alcohol support services when he is ready; bereavement support such as Cruse.

About 7 kg unintended weight loss and tiredness
Check for complete obstruction (saliva), food bolus, haematemesis or melaena — same-day if present

Widower eating alone and skipping meals
Guilt that his lifestyle may have caused this

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest that this is not simple reflux: “Food sticking that’s getting worse, with weight loss, needs a camera test urgently to find the cause — it may be a treatable narrowing, but it could be a cancer, and we need to know quickly.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your gullet as a pipe. Food catching more and more, week by week, tells me something may be narrowing it. Stronger antacids would be like putting a sign on the pipe — the camera lets us look inside and fix it.”

management.reflectIce: “After losing your friend the way you did, of course ‘reflux’ felt safer to say. Getting you seen quickly is how we replace the guessing with an answer.”
management.psychosocial: No blame for the smoking or drinking today; a soft-diet plan for a man eating alone; alcohol support offered later, when he is ready.
sharedPlan: NICE NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer because of the dysphagia — referral sent today
Face-to-face weight, abdominal and neck examination; FBC, U&E, LFTs — without delaying the referral
Soft, moist food little and often; dietitian if weight keeps falling
safetyNet: Food stuck and not passing, cannot swallow saliva, vomiting blood → A&E
Ring the surgery if no hospital date within a week; GP reviews the result with him

pitfalls.intro: Candidates rarely miss that dysphagia is a red flag once they hear it described — they lose marks by accepting “reflux” too early, by lecturing about alcohol, or by failing to hear the fear behind the jokes.

items.fail: Prescribing a PPI and reviewing in four weeks because he has a long reflux history.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG12 calls for a suspected cancer pathway referral for dysphagia at any age; the CG184 reflux pathway no longer applies.
items.fix: “Stronger tablets could hide this. Swallowing trouble means an urgent referral for a camera test — I’ll send it today.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he can swallow liquids or saliva, or about vomiting blood.
items.why: Complete obstruction and bleeding change the pathway to same-day care; examiners look for this screen.
items.fix: Two quick questions: “Can you still drink and swallow your own saliva? Any blood?”

items.fail: Waiting for bloods or an examination before sending the referral.
items.why: The referral criterion is met on history alone; tests are supportive and must not add delay.
items.fix: Send the referral today and book the examination and bloods alongside.

items.fail: Laughing along with “I could do with losing it”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The humour hides fear and unintended weight loss is a red flag.
items.fix: “You laughed about the weight — has anything in particular been worrying you?”

items.fail: A lecture on alcohol units and smoking in the middle of the explanation.
items.why: He already feels it is his fault; shaming reduces engagement and wastes time the plan needs.
items.fix: Record the history neutrally, remove the blame, and offer support at a later appointment.

items.fail: Leaving no plan for how he eats while he waits.
items.why: A widower skipping meals with dysphagia can lose weight and fluid quickly; a tailored plan scores.
items.fix: Soft, moist food little and often, weight check at the examination, dietitian if needed.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch” and no named emergency triggers.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no fallback for a lost referral are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name A&E triggers, “ring me if no date within a week”, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: He opens with reflux, age and stronger tablets, and jokes about the weight. Agree to explore the swallow first; flag the weight.
Onset, progression, solids versus liquids, level, pain, regurgitation, saliva, weight, bleeding. Smoking and alcohol asked neutrally.
Read the humour as a shield. The friend who died of throat cancer; guilt about the pub years. No blame.
Not reflux. NICE NG12: dysphagia → suspected cancer pathway referral (often straight to OGD), referral today. Face-to-face exam and bloods alongside. Soft diet.
Can’t swallow saliva, food stuck, vomiting blood → A&E. Ring if no date in a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a PPI or stronger antacid and reviews in a month; never characterises the swallow; lets the weight-loss joke pass; lectures about drink and smoking; no safety-net for complete obstruction.
wordPics.pass: Recognises progressive dysphagia with weight loss as a red flag; refers on the suspected cancer pathway under NICE NG12; asks about the key features and bleeding; acknowledges his worry; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: reads the humour as fear and surfaces his friend’s death; takes the guilt away rather than adding to it; explains why stronger tablets would be the wrong kindness; practical soft-diet plan for a man eating alone; clear fallback if the hospital date does not arrive; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Let’s try a stronger acid tablet for a month and see if the swallowing improves.”
avoid.instead: “Stronger tablets could cover this up. With swallowing trouble, the right step is an urgent referral for a camera test.”
avoid.why: NICE NG12 does not require a PPI trial before referring dysphagia; a trial is a recognised cause of delayed diagnosis.

avoid.dont: “Well, with thirty years of smoking and all that drinking, this isn’t a surprise.”
avoid.instead: “I’m not here to blame you. What matters today is getting you seen quickly.”
avoid.why: Shaming a frightened man with guilt already on his mind risks him not attending.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, it’s probably just a narrowing from the acid.”
avoid.instead: “It could well be something treatable — and because I can’t tell which, we check quickly.”
avoid.why: False reassurance undermines the urgency and the honesty the station rewards.

SCA_MODELS.why: States the NICE NG12 dysphagia criterion (a suspected cancer pathway referral) and what happens next, balanced honestly

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d also like to see you in person — to weigh you, feel your tummy and neck — and take a blood count and some routine bloods. None of that will hold up the referral; I’ll send it today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Examination and bloods alongside, not instead of, the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: How are you managing with meals at the moment, day to day?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the practical and nutritional impact

SCA_MODELS.text: Since the wife passed I mostly eat on my own. Easier to skip it, if I’m honest.

That’s useful to know. Until the test, go for softer, moist food — soups, stews, mash, yoghurt — little and often, and take your time. If the weight keeps dropping we can get dietitian advice. And the drink — we can talk about cutting down another day, when you’re ready. Today is about the test.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical interim plan; defers the alcohol conversation without ignoring it

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s fair. I’d rather know than keep guessing.

If food gets stuck and won’t go down, you can’t swallow your own spit, or you vomit blood — go to A&E straight away, don’t wait for the appointment. The hospital will phone you with a date; if you haven’t heard within a week, ring me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Emergency triggers and a clear fallback if the appointment doesn’t come

SCA_MODELS.text: Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
Camera test in the next two weeks, bloods and a check-up with you, soft food meantime, and A&E if it all gets stuck or I bring up blood.
Perfect. I’ll go through the result with you myself. Thank you for telling me about your friend — it helps.
SCA_MODELS.why: Commits to follow-up and closes with warmth

SCA_STEM.name: Brian Halloran
SCA_STEM.recent: Long reflux history, self-managed with over-the-counter antacids. Retired publican. Alcohol about 30 units a week. No recent bloods or weight on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment — “swallowing a bit off, wants something stronger for reflux”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Six weeks of progressive difficulty swallowing solids with 7 kg unintended weight loss is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise. NICE NG12 calls for a suspected cancer pathway referral for dysphagia at any age — no PPI trial first, and not stronger antacids.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7 (amended 2025): refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. This replaced the earlier urgent direct-access endoscopy route. Brian meets both limbs.

Food sticking that has worsened from solids over weeks points to a mechanical narrowing — tumour or peptic stricture. Intermittent difficulty with both solids and liquids from the start suggests a motility problem. Ask about level, pain on swallowing, regurgitation, cough on swallowing and liquids.

Long-standing reflux (Barrett’s oesophagus and adenocarcinoma), 30 pack-years of smoking and heavy drinking (squamous cell carcinoma), male sex and age. Their presence adds urgency; their absence would not remove it.

points.h: Do not treat it as reflux
points.t: NICE CG184 manages uncomplicated dyspepsia and reflux with lifestyle advice, a PPI trial and H. pylori testing. That pathway does not apply once dysphagia is present — escalating acid suppression delays the diagnosis.
In person: weight and BMI, hydration, neck and supraclavicular nodes, epigastric mass. FBC for anaemia, U&E if intake is poor, LFTs. None of this should hold up the endoscopy request.
Unable to swallow saliva, food stuck and not passing, vomiting blood or significant dehydration — same-day emergency assessment, not the suspected cancer pathway.
UK CMOs (2016): regular drinking should stay at or below 14 units a week. Record intake accurately and offer support later; a lecture now risks losing a frightened man from the pathway.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question on the swallowing; did not jump to prescribing; noted the joked-about weight loss for later.
Retired publican, smoking and alcohol history asked without blame, eating alone as a widower, how meals are going.
The laugh about weight, “it’s my own fault”, and the friend who died — each explored rather than passed over.
Idea (reflux or ageing), the hidden concern (the same throat cancer as his friend, and guilt), expectation of stronger antacids.
Face-to-face weight, abdominal and neck examination; FBC, U&E, LFTs; suspected cancer pathway referral (often straight to OGD).
Oesophageal or gastric cancer, peptic stricture, oesophagitis, motility disorder; progressive solid-food dysphagia weighed as mechanical.
Checked liquids and saliva, level, odynophagia, regurgitation, weight, bleeding; knows complete obstruction or haematemesis means same-day care.
States a suspected upper GI cancer picture needing an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral, not reflux, in plain language and without false certainty.
NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer; no PPI trial first; referral sent today.
Soft diet, weight monitoring and dietitian if needed; alcohol recorded and support offered later without shaming.
A&E triggers named, ring if no hospital date within a week, GP reviews the result, teach-back.

social.t: A widower who now eats alone and skips meals is at risk of further weight loss and dehydration while he waits; give simple soft-diet advice and watch his weight.

A lifetime in the pub trade shapes how he sees his drinking. Record units accurately, avoid blame, and offer brief intervention or support when he is ready (UK CMOs 2016: no more than 14 units a week).

legal.t: If sedation is used for the endoscopy he must not drive home; the unit will say how long to avoid driving. There is no DVLA notification for the investigation itself.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): see the patient in person when remote assessment cannot meet their needs safely — weight and examination here — without letting it delay the referral.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share what he needs to know honestly and at his pace, without false reassurance. Document the red flags, the referral and the safety-net.
Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals to confirm he is seen; the doctor who refers owns the follow-up of the result.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support and Guts UK for information while waiting; local alcohol support services when he is ready; bereavement support such as Cruse.

redFlags: Progressive dysphagia to solids over six weeks — food sticking behind the sternum
About 7 kg unintended weight loss and tiredness
Check for complete obstruction (saliva), food bolus, haematemesis or melaena — same-day if present
psychosocial: Retired publican; 30 pack-years (ex-smoker) and about 30 units a week
Widower eating alone and skipping meals
Guilt that his lifestyle may have caused this
ice: Idea: “It’s my reflux, or just getting older”
Concern: a friend died of throat cancer that started with food sticking

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest that this is not simple reflux: “Food sticking that’s getting worse, with weight loss, needs a camera test urgently to find the cause — it may be a treatable narrowing, but it could be a cancer, and we need to know quickly.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your gullet as a pipe. Food catching more and more, week by week, tells me something may be narrowing it. Stronger antacids would be like putting a sign on the pipe — the camera lets us look inside and fix it.”

management.reflectIce: “After losing your friend the way you did, of course ‘reflux’ felt safer to say. Getting you seen quickly is how we replace the guessing with an answer.”
management.psychosocial: No blame for the smoking or drinking today; a soft-diet plan for a man eating alone; alcohol support offered later, when he is ready.
sharedPlan: NICE NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer because of the dysphagia — referral sent today
Face-to-face weight, abdominal and neck examination; FBC, U&E, LFTs — without delaying the referral
Soft, moist food little and often; dietitian if weight keeps falling
safetyNet: Food stuck and not passing, cannot swallow saliva, vomiting blood → A&E
Ring the surgery if no hospital date within a week; GP reviews the result with him

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates rarely miss that dysphagia is a red flag once they hear it described — they lose marks by accepting “reflux” too early, by lecturing about alcohol, or by failing to hear the fear behind the jokes.

items.fail: Prescribing a PPI and reviewing in four weeks because he has a long reflux history.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG12 calls for a suspected cancer pathway referral for dysphagia at any age; the CG184 reflux pathway no longer applies.
items.fix: “Stronger tablets could hide this. Swallowing trouble means an urgent referral for a camera test — I’ll send it today.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he can swallow liquids or saliva, or about vomiting blood.
items.why: Complete obstruction and bleeding change the pathway to same-day care; examiners look for this screen.
items.fix: Two quick questions: “Can you still drink and swallow your own saliva? Any blood?”

items.fail: Waiting for bloods or an examination before sending the referral.
items.why: The referral criterion is met on history alone; tests are supportive and must not add delay.
items.fix: Send the referral today and book the examination and bloods alongside.

items.fail: Laughing along with “I could do with losing it”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The humour hides fear and unintended weight loss is a red flag.
items.fix: “You laughed about the weight — has anything in particular been worrying you?”

items.fail: A lecture on alcohol units and smoking in the middle of the explanation.
items.why: He already feels it is his fault; shaming reduces engagement and wastes time the plan needs.
items.fix: Record the history neutrally, remove the blame, and offer support at a later appointment.

items.fail: Leaving no plan for how he eats while he waits.
items.why: A widower skipping meals with dysphagia can lose weight and fluid quickly; a tailored plan scores.
items.fix: Soft, moist food little and often, weight check at the examination, dietitian if needed.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch” and no named emergency triggers.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no fallback for a lost referral are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name A&E triggers, “ring me if no date within a week”, and teach-back.
